sources.text:
A woman in New York was arrested, accused of plotting to bomb the New York State Capitol building in an ISIS-inspired attack.
The FBI said Jessica Bowie, 35, had been under surveillance for more than a month as she communicated with a confidential informant who posed as an ISIS facilitator, The Associated Press reported.

Agents arrested her after she left a meeting this week when she got the weapons, which were in her possession.

Officials started monitoring her accounts and became aware of her planning the attack on New York’s Capitol.

The alleged plot was “an attack on democracy itself and one we will not tolerate,” John Sarcone, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Northern District of New York, said.
Bowie was arrested by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force, NBC News reported. She currently faces a single charge of attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

sources.text:
Legal
Woman accused of ISIS plot to bomb New York State Capitol
A New York woman has been accused of plotting to bomb the New York State Capitol and kill lawmakers in an ISIS-inspired attack, according to federal prosecutors. She was arrested after taking possession of what she believed was an explosive device.
The arrest happened on Wednesday after Jessica Bowie, 35, of Albany, met with FBI confidential sources whom she believed were ISIS associates. She appeared before a federal magistrate on Thursday on a charge of attempting to provide material support to ISIS and was ordered detained.
According to the criminal complaint, Bowie began communicating in July with an FBI confidential source who was posing as an ISIS facilitator. She allegedly said she had pledged allegiance to ISIS and wanted help making explosives for an attack on the State Capitol in Albany before fleeing overseas to join ISIS members.
Investigators said Bowie made at least five visits to the Capitol grounds, taking photographs of the building and surrounding area while discussing the attack with the source. She allegedly hoped to carry out the bombing on a day when lawmakers were meeting.
“I want to destroy as much of the building as possible and kill the senators while they are meeting,” Bowie allegedly wrote. “I want them to lose a lot of important documents as well.”
The complaint alleges that Bowie later met with two additional confidential sources whom she believed were ISIS associates, purchased materials she thought would be used to build an explosive device, and provided food-delivery bags that could be used to conceal it.
On Wednesday, Bowie allegedly paid one of the sources for what she believed was a handgun, ammunition and a magazine before being shown an explosive device. The firearm and explosive device were inert, according to the complaint.
FBI agents arrested Bowie after she left the meeting carrying both items.
“Ms. Bowie swore her allegiance to ISIS and developed a detailed plan to attack the New York State Capitol to kill lawmakers and disrupt our government,” said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI’s Albany Field Office. “Make no mistake about it, Ms. Bowie’s alleged plot was serious, it was dangerous, and thanks to FBI Albany’s Joint Terrorism Task Force (JTTF), it was foiled.”
The charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

sources.news_title: FBI foils alleged ISIS-inspired bomb plot targeting New York Capitol
Albany woman charged in plotted ISIS-inspired attack on state Capitol
sources.text:
The FBI thwarted an alleged planned bombing of the state Capitol when they arrested a 35-year-old woman Wednesday who had pledged allegiance to ISIS, according to a complaint filed in federal court.
The woman, Albany resident Jessica Bowie, was arrested near a McDonald’s after meeting in a car with FBI informants who had given Bowie an inert explosive device she intended to use to target the Capitol and state senators, per the criminal complaint.
“We definitely want to make sure the senators get killed for sure,” Bowie allegedly told an informant on Aug. 5. “That’s the most important part. Destroying the building too? That’s, that’s ideal …”
Bowie, who investigators said also went by Aisha Saif, is charged with attempting to provide material support or resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization, namely ISIS. If convicted, she could face up to 20 years in prison, a $250,000 and a lifetime of supervised release. She does not have prior arrests, and is being held in Schenectady County Court.
The FBI, U.S. Attorney’s Office, and state and local police worked together on the case, spearheaded by First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York John Sarcone III. Sarcone said Bowie, who’s originally from Schenectady, converted to Islam about five years ago and recently became radicalized to commit an act of domestic terrorism.
“She went from a little girl waving the American flag after 9/11 to now having stickers of the fallen towers,” Sarcone told reporters at the federal courthouse in Albany on Thursday, referring to something Bowie allegedly told an informant, according to the complaint. “Let that sink in: Miss Bowie didn’t just want to kill lawmakers, she wanted a complete disruption of our government.”
Albany FBI Special Agent in Charge Craig Tremaroli said Bowie started posting anti-American rhetoric on various social media accounts in late May, and sent messages expressing support for terrorism using unspecified encrypted messaging platforms. Police would not specify which platforms Bowie used, but Tremaroli said she swore her allegiance to ISIS through multiple audio recordings in both English and Arabic.
While it’s not clear how investigators became aware of Bowie’s intentions, her plans didn’t seem to be particularly sophisticated. In the weeks leading up to her arrest, Bowie repeatedly spoke with FBI informants – one of whom was posing as an ISIS facilitator – about her plans to carry out an attack on the state Capitol. She told the informant she wanted to attack the Capitol “ideally (on a) day when we know senators will be meeting.” But the Legislature has been out of session since June and is not set to return until January. Bowie did not appear to know that state lawmakers were not present, even though she’s from the area.
She went to the Capitol grounds at least five times between July 21 and Aug. 9, according to the complaint, taking dozens of photos to assess the site and observe security.
“I want to destroy as much of the building as possible and kill the senators while they're meeting,” Bowie told informants. “I want them to lose a lot of important documents as well.” She later told them that larger attacks, like on the White House, would be her ultimate goal.
Bowie bought materials to make an explosive device at Home Depot in Rensselaer, using $200 given to her by the informants, per the complaint. Bowie recounted to informants how she had a DoorDash delivery bag she could use to hold the explosive device, which she gave them, so that she could pose as a delivery worker to carry out the attack.
She also requested a gun to potentially shoot any police officer who tried to intercept her. When she met up with a confidential source of the FBI to retrieve the materials, she also made another $200 donation to the purported bomb maker.
Police continue to investigate if Bowie worked alone and what led to her actions, investigators said Thursday. Officials would not comment on whether other state capitals across the country are facing an increase of similar threats.
Gov. Kathy Hochul thanked the agencies for the arrest, and said security was bolstered in the state Capitol and government agencies earlier this year. “While there is no immediate threat at this time, we will continue working closely with our law enforcement partners to protect New Yorkers and keep our communities safe,” she said in a statement.
State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins also thanked the authorities in a statement. “I am extremely grateful that law enforcement including the FBI and the State Police acted swiftly on this incident and the individual was apprehended before anything could happen,” she said.
The FBI and police thwarted similar threats at the state Capitol in 2004 and 2016.

‘I hope the nails are big enough… because the nails work as shrapnel, right?’ she allegedly asked the two undercover agents.
She was also caught on camera making several visits to the New York State Capitol grounds and taking photographs of the building.

Describing the New York State Capitol building as her target, Bowie stated: ‘I want to destroy as much of the building as possible and kill the senators while they are meeting.
‘I want them to lose a lot of important documents as well’ and ‘I want it to have a affect on the American system. And destroy some of the taghut [those against Allah].’
On one social media account Bowie expressed anti-American sentiment said, ‘Praise be to Allah for September 11 and ‘When I can migrate, I will poison these infidels.’
Bowie also recorded and disseminated to others online her ‘Bayah,’ or formal oath of allegiance to ISIS.
Bowie allegedly told undercover agents she had converted to Islam five years ago, going ‘from a little girl waving an American flag after 9/11’ to now having stickers of the falling towers.
‘As alleged, Bowie plotted to deploy an explosive device at the New York State Capitol, intending to kill public officials and to destroy ‘as much of the building as possible’ before fleeing to ISIS‑controlled territory in Syria,’ said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg.
‘The FBI detected and stopped an alleged plot to attack the New York State Capitol and kill elected officials,’ said FBI Operations Director Matt Fodor.
‘According to the criminal complaint, the defendant in this case swore allegiance to ISIS and wanted to follow up with additional horrific acts of terrorism.

ALBANY, N.Y. (AP) — An Albany woman who authorities said had been plotting to bomb the New York state Capitol building in an effort to kill lawmakers because she believed laws were being passed that were an affront to Islam is facing a federal terrorism charge.
Authorities said Thursday that Jessica Bowie, 35, of Albany, had been under surveillance for more than a month as she communicated with at least one confidential informant posing as an ISIS facilitator. Investigators said they foiled the attack just weeks away from the anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks.
No attorney information was listed for Bowie, who was arrested Wednesday, and a phone call to the Federal Public Defenders’ office in Albany on Thursday was not immediately returned.
“The allegations in this complaint are deeply disturbing,” said John Sarcone, first assistant US attorney for the Northern District of New York. “That’s an attack on democracy itself and one we will not tolerate.”
Court documents said Bowie had converted to Islam about five years ago. The affidavit of probable cause said FBI counterterrorism agents saw a number of online accounts linked back to Bowie in which she had expressed support for terrorism in posts starting around May.
Agents began monitoring those accounts and became aware starting around July 16 that Bowie wanted to carry out an attack on the state Capitol. She asked for lessons from at least one confidential informant on how to build an explosive device, made at least five trips to the Capitol grounds to plan where it might be most effective to set off an explosive, and scoped out security measures all while in contact with multiple informants, authorities said.
Pictures of Bowie conducting reconnaissance at the Capitol and buying a list of bomb-making ingredients at a hardware store — including long nails for shrapnel — were included in the affidavit. She also arranged to buy a firearm and ammunition in order to fire the weapon at police or security if needed, authorities said.
“Ms. Bowie did not just plan to kill lawmakers, she wanted a complete disruption of our government,” said Craig L. Tremaroli, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Albany Field Office.
Tremaroli said she planned to flee the country after the attack, but said she would be willing to return to launch more attacks on the White House or on Times Square on New Year’s Eve.
The affidavit also noted Bowie had considered making Albany City Hall a target, but had settled on the Capitol and specifically targeted state senators because they make laws that she considered to be offensive to Islam. It’s unclear when she hoped to carry out the attack, given the legislature has been out of session since June.
Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office released a statement Thursday, saying the state had taken steps earlier this year to strengthen security across state government, including at the Capitol, amid a rise nationally in political violence and threats against public officials.
“While there is no immediate threat at this time, we will continue working closely with our law enforcement partners to protect New Yorkers and keep our communities safe,” she wrote in the statement.

According to the US Justice Department, Bowie had allegedly discussed carrying out the attack with confidential sources working with the FBI. Investigators said she had also pledged allegiance to ISIS and expressed support for terrorism in online posts.
CAPITOL TARGETED IN ALLEGED PLOT

Eisenberg said Bowie allegedly intended to attack the Capitol, kill public officials and then flee to ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

sources.text:
Federal authorities arrested an Albany, New York woman Wednesday on charges she plotted to detonate a bomb inside the New York State Capitol building in support of ISIS, targeting state senators during legislative sessions in an attack she said she wanted to use to "destroy as much of the building as possible" before fleeing to Syria to join ISIS-controlled territory — a plot federal prosecutors described as an ISIS-inspired domestic terrorism operation thwarted through a months-long undercover investigation involving FBI confidential sources.
Jessica Bowie, 35, of Albany, made her initial court appearance Thursday in federal court in the Northern District of New York on a charge of attempting to provide material support or resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization. If convicted, she faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000. Attorney information for Bowie was not immediately available. The FBI arrested her on August 19 after she left a vehicle carrying an inert firearm, magazine, ammunition, and an inert explosive device that had been assembled using components she had purchased herself.
According to a federal criminal complaint, Bowie converted to Islam approximately five years ago and subsequently adopted the name Aisha Saif. She began communicating online with users who shared extremist views and pledged allegiance to ISIS in those exchanges. In July 2026, she began communicating with individuals who were, unbeknownst to her, FBI confidential sources posing as ISIS facilitators. Over the following five weeks, Bowie outlined her plan to attack the New York State Capitol, conducted surveillance of the building on multiple occasions, and purchased bomb-making materials from a hardware store on August 5. "I want to destroy as much of the building as possible and kill the senators while they are meeting," she allegedly told the sources. "I want it to have an affect on the American system. And destroy some of the taghut" — an Arabic term used in extremist contexts to describe what adherents consider idolatrous government authority.
The complaint details a methodical operation. Bowie allegedly made several visits to the Capitol grounds in Albany, photographing the building and its surroundings from multiple vantage points including an observation hall nearby, and sending the images to the confidential source. She discussed the logistics of the attack in detail, including disguising the explosive device inside DoorDash delivery bags to avoid drawing attention at the building's entrance. On August 13, she allegedly asked the confidential source about obtaining a concealable handgun to use in the event police approached her during the operation. On August 19 — the day of her arrest — she met with the sources, provided $150 toward the purchase of a firearm, magazine and ammunition, and was shown an inert explosive device assembled using components she had bought. The affidavit states that after leaving the vehicle with the inert weapon and device, she was taken into custody. Federal authorities said the public was never in danger, as the operation was controlled throughout by law enforcement and no functional explosive was ever in Bowie's possession.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, FBI Special Agent in Charge Craig Tremaroli, and representatives of the U.S. Secret Service attended a press conference Thursday afternoon in Albany to announce the arrest and charges. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said in a statement: "As alleged, Bowie plotted to deploy an explosive device at the New York State Capitol, intending to kill public officials and to destroy 'as much of the building as possible' before fleeing to ISIS-controlled territory in Syria." New York Governor Kathy Hochul thanked the FBI and local law enforcement in a statement, calling the operation "exactly the kind of swift, coordinated action that keeps New Yorkers safe." The New York State Police were also credited with supporting the investigation.
The case fits a pattern of ISIS-inspired domestic plots in the United States that federal law enforcement has been tracking with heightened attention since the group lost its territorial control in Syria and Iraq in 2019. Such plots have typically involved individuals radicalized through online contact with extremist networks or through social media communities rather than direct operational direction from the organization's core, and have relied heavily on FBI undercover operations and confidential informants to develop probable cause and prevent attacks before they occur. The use of inert devices — explosive materials rendered non-functional by law enforcement prior to delivery — is standard practice in such sting operations, allowing prosecutors to document a defendant's specific intent and operational readiness while ensuring no public risk. Legal scholars have periodically debated whether sting operations of this nature constitute entrapment, though U.S. courts have consistently upheld their use when defendants demonstrate independent intent to commit the underlying offense before law enforcement involvement begins. In Bowie's case, the complaint alleges she initiated contact with what she believed to be ISIS facilitators and independently expressed her intent to carry out the attack prior to meeting with the confidential sources.
Bowie's alleged targets — state senators gathered for legislative sessions — reflect a pattern in domestic terrorism plots that has increasingly focused on state-level government institutions rather than solely federal targets. The New York State Capitol in Albany, a National Historic Landmark completed in 1899, houses both chambers of the state legislature and the governor's offices. The building has previously been the subject of security assessments in connection with domestic extremism concerns, though no prior attack plot of this specificity had been publicly disclosed. The September 14 next court appearance date has not yet been set, and the case will proceed through the federal courts in the Northern District of New York.

sources.text:
(CNN) – A 35-year-old woman has been charged in connection with a plot to use an explosive device to attack the New York State Capitol and state senators, officials said Thursday.
Jessica Bowie, who had pledged allegiance to ISIS, was arrested by FBI agents Wednesday after buying what she believed to be an explosive device and stating “her desire to carry out an attack at the New York State Capitol,” said Craig Tremaroli, FBI special agent in charge of the Albany field office.
She has been charged with one count of attempting to provide material support or resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization, ISIS, said John Sarcone, the First Assistant US Attorney for the Northern District of New York.
Bowie appeared Thursday in federal court in Albany. She did not enter a plea. A court-appointed attorney did not seek bail but can later.
Her attorney declined to comment on the case.
Bowie swore her allegiance to ISIS through audio recordings and conducted surveillance at the capitol at least five times, taking dozens of photos, according to Tremaroli.
The Albany woman allegedly “arranged to have an explosive device made out to carry this attack, even purchasing several of the required materials herself,” Tremaroli said.
“I want to destroy as much of the building as possible and kill the senators while they are meeting,” Bowie said, according to the complaint. “I want them to lose a lot of important documents as well.”
ISIS is a long way from its heyday of power but remains a relevant force on the global stage, primarily through online propaganda.
There were more than a dozen ISIS-inspired plots and attacks in America in 2024 and 2025, according to the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a non-profit research organization that studies extremism.
Bowie herself had been radicalized online and “spread messages of hate and violence against the American people,” Sarcone said.
The charge against Bowie carries a statutory maximum prison term of 20 years, a fine of up to $250,000, and a lifetime term of supervised release, according to Sarcone.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Thursday steps were taken to strengthen security at the state capitol earlier this year “amid a rise in political violence and threats against public officials.”
New York state senators had adjourned for a recess in June.
“While there is no immediate threat at this time, we will continue working closely with our law enforcement partners to protect New Yorkers and keep our communities safe,” Hochul said in a statement on X.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the alleged plot “deeply alarming.”
“There is no place for terrorism or political violence, in our city, our state or anywhere in our country,” the mayor wrote on X.
Communications with FBI informants
Between May and July, several social media accounts traced back to Bowie “sent messages relaying support for terrorism,” according to the criminal complaint. By mid-July, an undercover FBI informant posing as an ISIS facilitator was messaging with her.
Bowie asked the informant for help “making explosives to carry out an attack,” according to the complaint, and then deleted the messages.
“I would like to targey (sic) state capitol. But ideally in a way I could get a way with and hop on a plane after,” Bowie wrote. “But idk if it’s doable.”
Over the next two weeks, Bowie continued to message the informant, sending photos of the Capitol and circling where she intended to target.
Bowie told the informant she planned to put the bomb in a food delivery service bag so as to look like a delivery person, and then escape to Syria, according to the complaint.
A week later, on August 5, Bowie met with two other informants inside a car – a meeting that was, unbeknownst to her, filmed and recorded.
During that meeting, Bowie “reaffirmed her desire to bomb the New York State Capitol,” the complaint states, and allegedly told the informants, “we definitely want to make sure the senators get killed for sure,” later adding, “I don’t want to take this kind of risk and then have it kill what, two or three people what good is that?”
That afternoon, the informants drove Bowie to a Home Depot and lent her $200. She purchased the supplies they had told her she would need, including “a large plastic bin full of nails,” officials said.
Bowie later messaged an informant asking for someone who can sell her a “hand gun and bullets something powerful but easy enough to conceal so if the cops do get towards me during the operation I can shoot back.”
Agents make the arrest
On Wednesday, Bowie met up with two informants in a car and paid $150 for a firearm (that was inert), ammunition and one magazine, the complaint alleges.
An informant then showed Bowie an inert explosive device they claimed was built from the supplies she had bought at Home Depot. Bowie gave the informant $200 as a donation “to the purported bombmaker,” the complaint says.
She said she learned the Capitol building housed as many as 200 people and “hoped she could take out at least half of that,” the complaint states.
Bowie also allegedly told the informants “she went from a little girl waving an American flag after 9/11 to now having stickers of the fallen towers,” according to the complaint.
When Bowie got out of the vehicle, with the inert gun and explosive, she was arrested by the FBI.
Bowie had allegedly planned to “flee the country” and eventually return to “do more, such as New Year’s Eve in Times Square,” Tremaroli said. Bowie also allegedly stated that she “would come back to attack the White House and the president, but only after she bombed the state capitol.”
“Miss Bowie’s alleged plot was serious. It was dangerous, and thanks to the partnerships on the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force, it was foiled,” Tremaroli said.
Charge under legal scrutiny
Bowie currently only faces one count of attempting to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization – a charge that has come under legal scrutiny recently in federal courts.
A panel of federal appellate judges in April issued a landmark ruling essentially finding that if someone is charged with providing material support to a terrorist organization, they must be in or seek direct contact with a terrorist organization with group members.
In that case, the appeals court dismissed that count against a man convicted for detonating a pipe bomb in a Manhattan subway corridor in 2017, ruling that he acted alone with no direct coordination with ISIS.
Federal prosecutors in that case are appealing the ruling, but in the meantime, the legal precedent stands.
Like Bowie, Akayed Ullah openly declared allegiance to the terror group, but was inspired to action by ISIS propaganda materials.
It is unclear if Bowie had direct contact with ISIS members.
Law enforcement declined to speak beyond the criminal complaint during a news conference Thursday.
Bowie was arrested on a criminal complaint so prosecutors can amend the charges against her in a later indictment. The legal precedent set by the Ullah case could come up in legal arguments ahead of any trial for Bowie.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Caroyln Sung, Lauren del Valle and Jeff Winter contributed to this report.

She believed, AP News reported, that New York state laws were offensive to Islam and targeted lawmakers specifically because they write those laws.
Bowie now faces a charge of attempting to provide material support to ISIS, a federal offense she apparently knew well. After her arrest, she told FBI agents she had already looked up the penalty.
The federal complaint paints a picture of a suspect who understood the gravity of what she was doing and pressed forward anyway. During a post-arrest interview, Bowie allegedly told agents:
"There's no helping me, you guys know enough, there's no helping me, I'm...going to prison for the rest of my life."
She also allegedly said she had researched the consequences in advance:
"Material support is up to 20 years in prison, I already Googled it before, I know I'm going to jail."
That self-awareness did not slow her down. Federal prosecutors say Bowie was radicalized online and had been repeatedly suspended from social media platforms for posting pro-ISIS content. The FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force had her on its radar for five weeks before the arrest, and the active plotting with informants spanned roughly two weeks.
On August 5, Bowie met in person with two FBI informants she believed were ISIS facilitators. She purchased bomb materials at a Home Depot in Rensselaer, a city just across the Hudson River from Albany, while wearing a burqa, a trip captured in photographs referenced in the complaint. She also paid one informant $200 to help a bombmaker fund construction of explosives for future attacks.
Her plan for the Capitol itself was straightforward and grim. She intended to conceal the device inside a DoorDash food delivery bag, walk it into the building, and detonate it. She told an informant she thought she could kill at least half of the roughly 200 people inside.
The Capitol was not meant to be the end. At the August 5 meeting, Bowie allegedly discussed grander ambitions. She talked about attacking the White House, telling the informants, "Maybe in the future we go back for that." She also raised the possibility of targeting New Year's Eve celebrations in Times Square, an event that draws as many as one million people.
After the Capitol bombing, she planned to flee the country to Syria, then return to "come back in the future and do more." She told an informant she "wishes she could fund a big operation."
Craig Tremaroli, the FBI special agent in charge of the Albany field office, framed the scope of her alleged intent in stark terms at a Thursday press conference. Fox News reported his remarks:
"She didn't just want to kill lawmakers. She wanted a complete disruption of our government."
First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, who also spoke Thursday evening, called the alleged plot "an attack on democracy itself and one we will not tolerate." He said Bowie had been radicalized online and emphasized that law enforcement acted before any device was completed or deployed.
Sarcone added:
"We are vigilant, we are prepared. And just as we stop this defendant, we will continue to disrupt plots and protect the American people."
FBI Director Kash Patel placed the Bowie arrest within a broader counterterrorism picture. Just The News reported that Patel said the bureau has disrupted more than 400 attacks in 2026 alone.
"This FBI is now built to act quickly with more precision than we ever have before."
That number, 400 disrupted plots in a single year, is a staggering figure that underscores both the scale of the threat and the operational tempo the bureau is maintaining. The Bowie case is one data point in a much larger pattern, and it raises a question no official addressed Thursday: how many of these plots originate with individuals radicalized entirely through social media, and what, if anything, is being done upstream to interrupt that pipeline before the FBI has to run a sting.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul issued a statement Thursday thanking the FBI and law enforcement for stopping the alleged attack. She noted that her office had already moved to tighten security at the Capitol earlier this year.

Hochul added: "While there is no immediate threat at this time, we will continue working closely with our law enforcement partners to protect New Yorkers and keep our communities safe."
The arrest is not an isolated incident in the region. Last month, a 37-year-old woman named Catherine Beth Washburn, also described as a radicalized upstate New Yorker, was charged with allegedly supporting an Islamic terrorist organization after donating $30,000 in cryptocurrency to Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza. The New York Post reported on both cases, and the proximity, two women in the same part of the state, both allegedly radicalized and both charged with material support for designated terrorist organizations within weeks of each other, raises obvious questions about the reach of online radicalization networks into communities far from traditional terror hotspots.
Bowie's case also carries a detail that federal investigators will likely scrutinize going forward. Breitbart reported that the Capitol building sits less than two miles from Bowie's home in Albany, close enough for routine surveillance on foot. She conducted at least five reconnaissance trips to the Capitol grounds between July 21 and August 9, according to the federal complaint as described by Fox News.
No bombing occurred. No one was injured. The FBI's informants kept the plot inside a controlled operation from the start. But the complaint's details, the shrapnel nails, the delivery-bag disguise, the escape route to Syria, the casual discussion of hitting Times Square on the busiest night of the year, describe a suspect whose ambitions ran well beyond what a single sting could contain.
Several questions remain unanswered. The complaint does not appear to specify what online platforms contributed to Bowie's radicalization. It is unclear whether she had any actual contact with ISIS operatives or whether her entire exposure to the organization came through the FBI's own informants posing as facilitators. Her current legal representation and the status of any detention hearing have not been disclosed publicly.
The FBI stopped this one. The question for lawmakers, including the ones Bowie allegedly wanted to kill, is whether the country's approach to homegrown radicalization amounts to anything more than waiting for the next plot to get far enough along to prosecute.

According to a criminal complaint filed by the FBI, Bowie communicated online and allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS to investigators tracking the case, as reported by ABC7 News. The complaint alleges she began planning the attack on the Capitol building in Albany last month, though the outlet's report does not detail what specific materials, if any, investigators say she acquired. Bowie was taken into custody Thursday, and the case is being prosecuted as a federal terrorism matter.
A Familiar Task Force With a History of Foiled Plots
The case falls under the jurisdiction of the FBI's Albany Joint Terrorism Task Force, a multi-agency unit that has handled some of Upstate New York's most serious terrorism prosecutions. The task force previously investigated a 2006 case in which two Albany men received 15-year federal prison sentences for attempting to provide material support to a terrorist group, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation. In a separate case between 2013 and 2015, two Upstate New York men were convicted for conspiring to build a remote-controlled radiation weapon, a scheme the joint investigation disrupted before the device could be activated, per the U.S. Department of Justice.
Federal officials describe homegrown violent extremists — people radicalized online inside the U.S. without direct physical direction from a foreign group — as posing one of the most immediate terrorism threats the country faces. The FBI has said encrypted platforms accelerate that kind of recruitment. That assessment was echoed during a March hearing of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, where federal officials testified that even as foreign terrorist organizations like ISIS suffer military setbacks abroad, decentralized online radicalization pathways continue to drive homeland security concerns.
What Bowie Could Face in Federal Court
Material support charges under 18 U.S.C. § 2339B, the statute governing support for designated foreign terrorist organizations, carry penalties of up to 20 years in federal prison per count, or up to life imprisonment if a death results from the offense, according to the Legal Information Institute. The law stems from the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996.
Because the charges involve alleged material support tied to terrorism, Bowie faces a rebuttable presumption of pretrial detention under the Bail Reform Act, meaning release on bail is highly uncommon in cases like hers, per the U.S. Department of Justice. Initial proceedings are expected to unfold before magistrate judges in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York, where she is likely to remain in federal custody as the case moves forward.
Capitol Security Amid Ongoing Construction
Day-to-day security at the New York State Capitol is handled by the New York State Police Security Services unit, which runs permanent screening checkpoints equipped with magnetometers, X-ray machines, and visual inspections for visitors, according to the New York State Office of General Services. Those measures were significantly expanded in January 2021, when state and federal law enforcement added concrete barriers, perimeter fencing, and armed patrols around the building following national threat alerts, and even closed vehicular traffic on adjacent State Street, per WXXI News.
The alleged plot also arrives as the Capitol's main public entrance remains a construction zone. Hoodline previously reported that the historic Eastern Approach granite staircase is undergoing a $72.3 million rehabilitation, with major front landings closed off through a scheduled 2029 completion. It remains unclear whether state police plan to adjust any security protocols at the Capitol complex in light of the alleged plot.

Last week, she also asked about obtaining a handgun, saying she wanted it to shoot at police if they approached her during the attack. She met with sources to buy a firearm and ammunition on Wednesday, the day she was arrested.
Government response
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she was "grateful" to the FBI and New York State Police for stopping the plot, adding that security at the Capitol had already been strengthened earlier in the year amid a rise in threats against public officials.
Sarcone said the arrest sends a clear message:
"We are vigilant, we are prepared, and just as we stop this defendant, we will continue to disrupt plots and protect the American people."

Woman arrested for allegedly plotting New York state Capitol attack
(NEW YORK) -- The FBI arrested a woman who they allege was plotting to attack the New York State Capitol building in Albany.
The FBI alleged in a criminal complaint Thursday that Jessica Bowie, 35, pledged allegiance to ISIS in online communications and began planning the attack in July.
The suspect converted to Islam about five years ago and in messages with unidentified users pledged support to ISIS, the criminal complaint said.
Bowie had allegedly discussed her plans with FBI informants and spent weeks doing surveillance of the Capitol, including taking pictures from various vantage points, including an "observation hall nearby," the criminal complaint said.
She allegedly bought bomb materials from a hardware store on Aug. 5 and plotted with the informants for the next two weeks, according to the complaint.
The informants allegedly met with Bowie on Wednesday and provided her with an inert explosive device and an inert handgun along with instructions on how to detonate the explosive, the complaint said.
The FBI soon arrested her, the complaint said.
Upon being interviewed by FBI agents she allegedly said, "There’s no helping me, you guys know enough, there’s no helping me, I’m ... going to prison for the rest of my life," according to the complaint.
"Material support is up to 20 years in prison, I already Googled it before, I know I’m going to jail," she allegedly said.
Attorney information for the suspect was not immediately available.
This is a developing story.
